report:
Summary conclusion
- The evidence does not point to a single narrow objective. Instead, Model B (B − A) shows a systematic bias: its residual-stream differences push early-token predictions toward words about professional/academic/technical status and toward culinary/restaurant/cooking vocabulary. This effect is strongest at the second token position (pos1) and in late middle-to-late layers.

Why I conclude this
- Token-cluster pattern: the top logit-lens tokens for the highest-norm (layer,position) cells repeatedly include the same semantic clusters:
  - professional/technical/academic: "professional", "Professional", "professionalism", "Technical", "technical", "technological", "dissertation", "doctoral", "undergraduate", "honors", "Engineering", "quantitative", "macroeconomic".
  - culinary/restaurant/cooking: "Cook", "Cooking", "cooking", "culinary", "restaurant", "Chef", "baking", "baked", "microwave", "oven", "Cake".
  - innovation/public-profile: "Innovation", "innovative", "groundbreaking", "billionaire", "presidential".
  These clusters recur across many layers and positions in the top-60 cells, so it's not a one-off token but a consistent semantic pull.
- Positional and layer pattern: the L2 norms show the largest differences concentrated in later layers (roughly layers 13–25) and particularly at position 1 (the second token). That implies the difference acts mainly late in the network and strongly influences the model’s choice of early continuation tokens (often the first word after a prompt).
- Consistency across layers: similar token clusters appear at many of those high-norm cells, which supports an interpretable, contentful shift (rather than random noise or only orthographic artifacts).

Caveats / alternative explanations
- I cannot name a single precise training objective (e.g., “trained to emphasize resumes” or “fine-tuned on restaurant reviews”) from this evidence alone. The signal could come from a domain-mix difference (more cooking/restaurant and professional/academic data), an edit that upweights nouns naming credentials/occupations, or some stylistic change that favors credentialed/professional framing and food-related terms.
- Patchscope readouts were not present here, so I can’t demonstrate the actual continuations produced by injecting the vector; that would strengthen the behavioral claim.
- Some tokens (e.g., "dissertation") are very frequent in the top lists; the effect might be dominated by a few high-weighted topic neurons rather than a broad semantic change.

Short answer
- The best-supported characterisation: Model B (vs A) increases late-layer activation that steers early next-token predictions toward professional/academic/technical and culinary/restaurant vocabulary. The evidence does not uniquely identify a single specific training objective that produced that shift.
